title: Atlas Insurance - reference call readiness check (boundaries + champions)
summary: Readiness check to confirm Atlas stakeholder support for participating as a Redwood reference customer (reference calls first, public case study later). Atlas confirmed Priyom and Dana can participate on calls, with Vendor Management (Leah) requesting guardrails: no pricing disclosure, no internal incident details, avoid naming competitors unprompted, and exclude direct Atlas competitors as prospects. We aligned on proof points that resonate with Atlas peers (finserv/regulated): reliability under load, p95 latency consistency, fallback behavior, auditability, and predictable cost controls. Next steps: Redwood to send a one-page call brief + proposed boundaries in writing; Atlas to confirm internal approvals and identify a backup speaker; target first reference call in ~2–3 weeks for a late-stage Dedicated/Private prospect.
topics: Proof points: latency consistency, reliability/fallbacks, auditability
What Atlas can/can’t share (metrics, architecture, pricing)
Follow-up assets: reference call brief + approved talk track
action_items: Avery Johnson - Send Atlas a draft reference-call boundaries doc + 1-page brief template for review - due 2025-10-14
Markus Klein - Provide a short technical 'what to emphasize / what to avoid' section (fallbacks, eval harness, deployment scope) for the brief - due 2025-10-14
Priyom Das - Confirm internal greenlight for participating in up to 1 call/month and nominate a backup speaker - due 2025-10-17
Leah Martinez - Validate any vendor/legal requirements for reference calls under mutual NDA and share language if needed - due 2025-10-17
next_steps: Redwood to circulate a written boundaries + logistics doc (who can attend, what can be shared, no-go topics).
Atlas to confirm approved metrics format (exact numbers vs ranges) for verbal reference calls.
Schedule a 20–25 min “pilot” reference call with a qualified late-stage prospect; Redwood to provide questions in advance.
transcript:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Date: 2025-10-10
Time: 3:30pm ET
Duration: 34 min
Title: Atlas Insurance - reference call readiness check (boundaries + champions)
Organizer: Avery Johnson (Redwood Inference)

Attendees:
- Avery Johnson (Redwood) - Enterprise AE
- Markus Klein (Redwood) - Solutions Engineering
- Priyom Das (Atlas Insurance) - Director, AI Platform
- Dana Cho (Atlas Insurance) - ML Engineering Manager
- Leah Martinez (Atlas Insurance) - Vendor Management

---

[00:00] Avery Johnson: Alright, I think we’re recording. Thanks everybody for making time. The goal today is pretty simple: make sure we’re set up for success if we do a reference call with a prospect. So confirm who’s comfortable speaking, what proof points matter to your peers, and importantly what you do not want to get asked about.

[00:19] Priyom Das: Yep, makes sense.

[00:21] Leah Martinez: And from my side, just want to ensure we’re not committing to anything outside what we’re allowed to share.

[00:26] Markus Klein: Totally. We can keep this very bounded.

[00:30] Avery Johnson: Cool. Priyom, maybe quick check—do you have internal support for doing a couple reference conversations? I know we had discussed “lightweight” first, not a public case study yet.

[00:41] Priyom Das: Yeah, so, internally I have support from our VP Engineering. The caveat is we need to treat it like vendor reference calls we’ve done before: late-stage only, mutual NDA, and no numbers that could be interpreted as, like, financial disclosures.

[00:56] Avery Johnson: That’s consistent with what we see. When you say late-stage, is that like… evaluation done, security done, procurement happening?

[01:04] Priyom Das: Exactly. If it’s an early-stage fishing expedition, we don’t do it.

[01:09] Leah Martinez: And also no direct competitors. If it’s another large carrier, that’s a hard no.

[01:14] Avery Johnson: Got it—no other major insurers. We can screen that on our side.

[01:18] Markus Klein: Also we can do it so you don’t see who it is until we confirm category and stage. Like “regulated fintech, late-stage Dedicated” and then you can say yes/no.

[01:27] Dana Cho: Yeah, that would help.

[01:30] Avery Johnson: Great. On champions—who should be the primary voice? Priyom, you, Dana—anyone else we should plan to have as backup?

[01:39] Priyom Das: I can do it. Dana can cover more of the engineering day-to-day. Backup could be… maybe someone from SRE, but they’re stretched.

[01:48] Dana Cho: If the questions get deep on like load patterns or incident stuff, I’d prefer not to speak for SRE. But I can speak to what we saw during the cutover and how stable it’s been.

[01:58] Avery Johnson: That’s fair. We should avoid incident-level specifics anyway.

[02:02] Leah Martinez: Yes, please. No incident details.

[02:05] Markus Klein: We can keep it at “we require high availability and we observed consistent latency post-migration,” that kind of thing.

[02:12] Avery Johnson: Perfect. Let’s talk proof points. If I’m an engineering leader at another regulated company, what matters most for me to hear from Atlas about Redwood?

[02:24] Priyom Das: Consistency. Not just best-case p50 but the p95 staying in bounds when traffic spikes. We were getting variability before.

[02:32] Dana Cho: Yeah. The big difference for us was not having to babysit. The fallback behavior was… I mean, it did what it said. We had a couple windows where capacity was tight and the policy routed to the compatible model. We didn’t have app outages.

[02:47] Markus Klein: That’s helpful. So reliability and graceful degradation. Anything on cost?

[02:52] Priyom Das: Cost matters, but we have to be careful. We can say “we reduced waste” or “we improved cost predictability.” But we cannot share our exact $ per million tokens, and definitely not our overall spend.

[03:05] Avery Johnson: Understood. Would ranges be OK? Like “we saw a reduction on the order of tens of percent”?

[03:11] Leah Martinez: That’s the kind of language we usually allow, but it depends. For a verbal reference, ranges are sometimes acceptable if they’re not tied to volumes.

[03:21] Priyom Das: I’d prefer to keep it qualitative on cost and quantitative on reliability/latency if we can.

[03:27] Markus Klein: Quantitative on latency as in “p95 went from X to Y” or more like “p95 below 800ms for our typical prompts”?

[03:34] Dana Cho: More the second. Like “we set a p95 target and we were able to consistently hit it.” I don’t want to give a before/after with exact numbers on a call with strangers.

[03:46] Avery Johnson: Makes sense. We can craft a talk track that’s “targets + achieved,” without revealing your baseline stack too much.

[03:53] Priyom Das: Exactly.

[03:55] Avery Johnson: On security/compliance—what can you say publicly or in a reference call?

[04:00] Leah Martinez: In a mutual NDA call, we can talk about security posture at a high level. We can say we required audit logs, encryption, key management integration. But we should not say anything like “Atlas is configured exactly this way” or “we store logs for X years,” unless we’ve approved it.

[04:16] Markus Klein: Got it. So focus on capabilities and requirements, not your internal settings.

[04:20] Dana Cho: Also we can mention we’re in a VPC deployment model, but not the cloud account details obviously.

[04:26] Avery Johnson: Yep. VPC/Private is fine as a concept. We’ll avoid provider specifics unless you want to name it.

[04:33] Priyom Das: Let’s not name cloud provider, if possible.

[04:36] Avery Johnson: OK. We can keep it “private deployment” and move on.

[04:40] Markus Klein: For proof points beyond latency and reliability, do you want to mention evaluation? Like how you validated output quality while optimizing?

[04:48] Priyom Das: That’s actually a good one. Our peers will ask: “how did you prevent regressions when you changed serving?” We can say we ran a prompt set, did diffing, and monitored quality.

[05:00] Dana Cho: Yeah, we used our harness plus your eval hooks. But again, we don’t want to go deep into what our prompt set is.

[05:07] Markus Klein: Totally. Just the fact that there was an evaluation loop.

[05:10] Avery Johnson: Great. Let’s list “safe” proof points:
- Reliability under load, consistent p95
- Fallback/routing prevented outages
- Private deployment met security/audit requirements
- Evals/monitoring prevented quality regressions
- Operational overhead reduced
Does that feel right?

[05:28] Priyom Das: Yes.

[05:29] Leah Martinez: Add “vendor support responsiveness,” maybe. That comes up a lot.

[05:33] Avery Johnson: Good call. Support SLA and responsiveness.

[05:37] Markus Klein: And we can keep “support” to “we had access to solutions engineers during rollout” rather than anything contractual.

[05:44] Leah Martinez: Right.

[05:45] Avery Johnson: Now the “avoid list.” Leah you already said no pricing, no incident details, no competitor comparisons. Anything else?

[05:55] Priyom Das: No roadmap promises. Like don’t put us in a position where we’re saying “Redwood will deliver feature X next quarter.”

[06:03] Markus Klein: Yep, we’ll avoid roadmap.

[06:06] Dana Cho: Also avoid sharing our traffic volumes. That’s sensitive.

[06:10] Avery Johnson: Got it—no token volumes, no QPS numbers.

[06:14] Leah Martinez: And no naming internal teams beyond general roles.

[06:18] Avery Johnson: Makes sense.

[06:20] Markus Klein: What about naming your previous vendor? Sometimes prospects ask “who did you switch from?”

[06:25] Priyom Das: We can say “we evaluated a few options,” but we should not name them. That’s part of our vendor policy.

[06:32] Avery Johnson: Understood.

[06:35] Avery Johnson: On the reference call format—what works for you? Typically we do 20–25 minutes, Redwood hosts, we do intros, we remind everyone it’s under NDA, and we keep it to a set of questions. Does that fit?

[06:49] Dana Cho: Yes, as long as we get the questions ahead of time.

[06:53] Priyom Das: And we want the right to stop the conversation if it goes off rails.

[06:58] Avery Johnson: 100%. We’ll set that expectation with the prospect.

[07:03] Leah Martinez: Also a cap on frequency. We can’t be doing this weekly.

[07:08] Avery Johnson: Totally. What’s reasonable? One per month? Two per quarter?

[07:13] Priyom Das: One per month is fine, with a cooldown if it becomes burdensome.

[07:18] Avery Johnson: Great, we’ll adopt “max one call per month unless Atlas opts in otherwise.”

[07:24] Markus Klein: And we can rotate speakers, Priyom vs Dana, depending on topic.

[07:28] Dana Cho: Works.

[07:31] Avery Johnson: For prospect qualification: you said no other insurers. What about adjacent—payments, banking, healthcare?

[07:39] Priyom Das: Banking is okay. Payments okay. Healthcare probably okay. Just not P&C insurance or life insurance direct.

[07:48] Avery Johnson: Got it.

[07:49] Markus Klein: And stage must be late. We can set criteria: security review underway, reference is a gating step.

[07:56] Leah Martinez: Yes.

[07:58] Avery Johnson: Perfect. I’ll ask Tyler on our side to make sure we log these rules in the intake process.

[08:05] Markus Klein: One more question: are there any specific “peer questions” you think will come up that we should prepare you for?

[08:12] Priyom Das: They’ll ask about uptime and how you handle region failures.

[08:17] Dana Cho: They’ll ask “what happens when the model is slow,” like tail latency. So they’ll ask about batching and caching too.

[08:25] Markus Klein: Great. We can give you a simple answer framework: “We worked with Redwood on configuration—batching, cache—and we set SLOs and monitored.”

[08:35] Priyom Das: Exactly.

[08:37] Leah Martinez: And make sure we don’t claim absolute guarantees unless it’s in contract.

[08:42] Avery Johnson: Yes, no absolute language.

[08:45] Avery Johnson: Quick check: do you want to bring up that this started as a Dedicated evaluation and moved toward Private? Or is that too much detail?

[08:55] Priyom Das: You can say “we evaluated Dedicated and Private deployment options and chose private for our requirements.” That’s fine.

[09:02] Dana Cho: That’s safe.

[09:04] Markus Klein: Great.

[09:06] Avery Johnson: Okay, last thing—next steps. I’ll send a one-page brief for your review: who you are, what you can say, what you can’t, and a “suggested answers” section. Then we’ll treat the first call as a pilot.

[09:19] Priyom Das: Sounds good.

[09:21] Leah Martinez: Please include the mutual NDA assumption in writing.

[09:25] Avery Johnson: Will do.

[09:26] Markus Klein: And I’ll add a technical do/don’t list so you’re not put on the spot.

[09:31] Dana Cho: Thank you.

[09:33] Avery Johnson: Anything else we missed?

[09:36] Priyom Das: That’s it. Appreciate making this structured.

[09:40] Avery Johnson: Great. Thanks everyone.

---

Auto-generated Notes (may be incomplete):
- Key boundary constraints: no pricing/spend, no traffic volumes, no incident details, do not name competitors or previous vendor, avoid roadmap promises, avoid cloud provider naming.
- Eligible prospects: late-stage only, mutual NDA required, not direct Atlas competitors (no other insurers).
- Target proof points: p95 consistency, reliability/fallback behavior, private deployment/security requirements, eval/monitoring discipline, support responsiveness.
